name: KY-016 RGB LED module
description: Full-colour 5 mm RGB LED module: one common-cathode RGB LED with a current-limiting resistor (150 Ω on most boards) already fitted in series with each colour. Drive R, G and B high (3.3–5 V) to light red, green and blue; PWM each pin to mix colours. Red Vf about 1.8 V, green/blue about 2.8 V, 20 mA rated per colour. Sold as: KY-016 / HW-479 RGB LED module (common 37-in-1 kit clone, 3 × 150 Ω onboard resistors), 4-pin header -, R, G, B.
eli5: Three little lights (red, green, blue) in one bulb: switch each colour on with its own pin, and mix them to make any colour.

pins.description: Common cathode of the RGB LED: connect to GND

pins.name: R
pins.description: Red LED anode (through the onboard resistor): high = red on, PWM for brightness

pins.name: G
pins.description: Green LED anode (through the onboard resistor): high = green on, PWM for brightness

pins.name: B
pins.description: Blue LED anode (through the onboard resistor): high = blue on, PWM for brightness

buildNotes: Wire - to GND and R, G, B to three GPIOs. The resistors are on the board, so no extra resistors are needed on the HW-479 / 150 Ω version.
From a 3.3 V GPIO with the 150 Ω resistors: red about (3.3 - 1.8) / 150 = 10 mA, green and blue only about 3 mA, so blue and green look dimmer than red. Lower the red PWM duty to balance white.

Some KY-016 boards use 1 kΩ resistors (marked 102) and are much dimmer; that is normal. The Joy-IT version is documented without onboard resistors: check for the three small SMD resistors, and if there are none add 180 Ω (red) and 100 Ω (green, blue) in series.
Common cathode: a GPIO high turns a colour ON. (Common-anode RGB LEDs are the other way round.)
Some clones print - G R B instead of - R G B. Read the silkscreen; if colours come out swapped, swap the pin numbers in code.

example.code:
from machine import Pin
import time

# KY-016 is common cathode: a pin HIGH turns that colour ON
red = Pin({R}, Pin.OUT, value=0)
green = Pin({G}, Pin.OUT, value=0)
blue = Pin({B}, Pin.OUT, value=0)

def colour(r, g, b, name):
    red.value(r)
    green.value(g)
    blue.value(b)
    print(name)

while True:
    colour(1, 0, 0, 'RED')
    time.sleep(1)
    colour(0, 1, 0, 'GREEN')
    time.sleep(1)
    colour(0, 0, 1, 'BLUE')
    time.sleep(1)
    colour(0, 0, 0, 'OFF')
    time.sleep(1)

test.title: Red, green and blue light in turn, then all go off
